notes.title: Choose checked exceptions for actionable recovery, runtime exceptions for contract violations
notes.core: Categorize failures by the response that a reasonable caller can take. Checked exceptions advertise an expected and actionable exceptional recovery path. Runtime exceptions normally signal a programming error or violated precondition. Errors are generally not recoverable application conditions.
rules: Use checked exceptions for conditions outside the caller’s direct control when the caller has a realistic, meaningful recovery action; provide enough structured context for that action.
Use IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, NullPointerException or another suitable runtime contract error when an API precondition/invariant is violated by the programmer.
Never catch Error as ordinary business-failure handling; VM failures and linkage errors should normally propagate to supervision/restart policy.
Keep a documented distinction between a normal absence outcome, a recoverable exceptional condition, and a bug.
Avoid blanket catch(Exception) or a generic return code that erases whether retry, correction, or escalation is appropriate.
Design recoverability at the API boundary, not by declaring every potentially failed operation a checked exception.
nuance: A network or remote-service outage can have recoverable cases, but a caller who cannot reasonably act should not be forced into a meaningless checked catch.
Runtime exceptions can arise from environment or implementation faults as well as caller mistakes; the design category is guidance, not a universal causal diagnosis.
An unchecked exception is not inherently ignorable; include operational telemetry, error mapping and causality across boundaries.
Do not disguise fatal errors such as OutOfMemoryError as routine transactions to retry repeatedly.
Java 21 sealed result hierarchies can represent expected business outcomes; they are not a universal replacement for genuinely exceptional failures.
notes.misconception: Every failure should be checked so that every caller can catch it—or every failure should be unchecked so that callers are never bothered.
notes.production_context: A payout adapter distinguishes invalid amount (contract error), a temporarily unavailable settlement endpoint (potentially recoverable transport exception), and an unsupported JVM/runtime condition (not a business outcome).
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 preserves the checked/unchecked distinction; modern sealed results and records can model ordinary states without converting unexpected faults into successful responses.

notes.title: Keep checked exceptions scarce and useful, not ceremonial
notes.core: A checked exception has value only when clients can reasonably recover or are meaningfully required to consider a failed operation. Do not add a checked type merely to force repetitive pass-through or empty catch blocks.
rules: Before adding checked throws, identify what a caller can actually do and how the exception helps choose that recovery.
For ordinary missing values from a valid query, prefer a documented empty result or Optional rather than a checked no-result exception when absence is normal.
Consider splitting a risky operation into a pure condition test and state-changing action only when doing so is safe against races and external state changes.
Use a structured result or an unchecked abstraction-specific failure when checked handling would be boilerplate with no actionable response.
Preserve an unavoidable recoverable I/O exception where handling retry/cancel/alternate resource is a real client obligation.
Do not suppress causes or silently return defaults merely to eliminate a checked throws clause.
nuance: Test-then-act may introduce a time-of-check/time-of-use race; a filesystem existence check cannot guarantee the subsequent open succeeds.
Unchecked does not mean acceptable to ignore; observability, backoff and appropriate user feedback remain important.
Adding a checked exception to a widely implemented public interface may impose extensive source compatibility work.
An Optional value is for ordinary absence, not for replacing connection failures, authorization denial or timeout errors.
A truly checked exception is valuable when recoverability is substantial even though it makes APIs and lambda use more verbose.
notes.misconception: Removing throws from an API automatically improves correctness, even when the operation can fail for reasons callers must address.
notes.production_context: A merchant lookup returns Optional<Merchant> for an unknown merchant; a separate network request can report a checked failure when the caller must choose retry, fallback or cancellation.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 retains checked exception enforcement and Optional APIs; modern record/sealed results allow typed domain responses but do not make I/O and concurrency races disappear.

notes.title: Prefer familiar standard exceptions whose contracts fit the failure
notes.core: Reuse the standard Java exception vocabulary so callers can interpret failures consistently without importing a one-off type for every minor contract violation.
rules: Use IllegalArgumentException for an unacceptable non-null argument and NullPointerException for a required reference that is null when the API uses that convention.
Use IllegalStateException when the receiver has a state that disallows the requested operation, independently of the value of the argument.
Use IndexOutOfBoundsException for invalid positional indices and UnsupportedOperationException when an operation is intentionally unavailable.
Use ConcurrentModificationException only for appropriate detected invalid concurrent modifications, not as a universal concurrency-error label.
Reuse these standard exceptions in public contracts unless a distinct domain exception adds material recovery information.
Avoid throwing a broad Exception, RuntimeException or Throwable when a precise standard category exists.
nuance: NullPointerException is often automatically produced by JVM dereference; explicit Objects.requireNonNull improves failure locality for public contracts.
A failed optimistic database version check may merit a domain conflict result rather than pretending it is a Java collection ConcurrentModificationException.
UnsupportedOperationException is about a deliberately unsupported operation, not an overload for temporary service unavailability.
NoSuchElementException is suitable where an API contract requires an element but none exists; an ordinary query may prefer Optional instead.
Standard exception reuse is about meaning and API predictability, not hard-coded exact message text or an invented exception hierarchy.
notes.misconception: Any RuntimeException is an equivalent signal to callers, so using generic RuntimeException everywhere is sufficient.
notes.production_context: A reconciliation query rejects negative offsets with IndexOutOfBoundsException, a closed uploader rejects submissions with IllegalStateException, and a read-only view refuses mutation with UnsupportedOperationException.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 preserves these standard exception families and offers Objects bounds checks for index contracts; failure semantics must still match the actual public API.

notes.title: Translate lower-level exceptions only when the abstraction warrants it
notes.core: Public APIs should expose failures meaningful in their own abstraction. Translate an alien lower-level exception into a fitting higher-level type when necessary, preserving the original cause and avoiding speculative wrapping of every failure.
rules: Map a lower-level failure to a higher-level exception when the dependency-specific type misrepresents the public method’s contract.
Preserve the root cause using an appropriate cause constructor or initCause so diagnostics can identify the original source.
Avoid broad catch-and-wrap of every RuntimeException because it conceals bugs and creates misleading domain failure categories.
Favor designing the lower-level operation to prevent the alien exception where a cleaner interface can do so.
Keep source-specific failures out of cross-layer APIs when caller isolation and compatibility benefit, but do not erase their diagnostic detail.
Use the abstraction’s documented nullability, absence and validation contract instead of blindly translating programming errors.
nuance: NoSuchElementException from an iterator may translate to IndexOutOfBoundsException for a positional list API, depending on its documented contract.
An exception wrapper should avoid duplicating sensitive data in public messages while still preserving bounded diagnostics.
A nested cause chain is useful only if upper layers deliberately communicate the correct failure category to the caller.
A checked lower-level exception can be wrapped in a domain checked or runtime exception depending on the higher-level recoverability requirement.
Preventing invalid state at the lower layer can be better than adding another translation catch around every operation.
notes.misconception: Catching every exception and rethrowing a generic service exception is always good abstraction hygiene.
notes.production_context: A merchant ledger adapter maps an out-of-range storage cursor into its documented paging exception and retains the storage-side cause for internal diagnostics, without recategorizing unrelated programming failures.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 supports standard Throwable cause chains and typed exceptions; current records/sealed results may model normal alternatives, but error translation still needs contract review.

notes.title: Document checked and unchecked exception contracts deliberately
notes.core: Exception behavior is part of a public contract. Document important checked and unchecked failures, their exact preconditions and recovery intent so callers can use APIs correctly, and verify that code and Javadoc agree.
rules: Declare each checked exception that a method can propagate through its public checked contract instead of hiding it behind a vague catch.
Document important unchecked exceptions with @throws in Javadoc, including meaningful null, range and illegal-state preconditions.
Document specific circumstances for each failure; names alone do not tell callers what they must avoid or recover from.
Keep comments consistent with actual thrown types; verify important branches with executable contract tests.
Avoid a single ambiguous @throws Exception or redundant throws clause that conceals a caller-actionable distinction.
Use generated Javadoc/doclint to catch syntax and missing-tag problems, while recognizing that clean tooling cannot prove semantic accuracy.
nuance: Unchecked exceptions need not appear in a Java throws clause; this does not exempt significant API failure behavior from documentation.
An implementation may internally catch or translate a checked exception, so document what can actually escape the public boundary.
Javadoc inheritance and @implSpec should be checked for changes in overrides and subclass-specific behavioral contracts.
A public checked throws change can break source clients and lambdas; review compatibility before widening an API.
Privacy/security rules still apply to error messages: do not document unstable internal messages or leak raw secrets in diagnostics.
notes.misconception: Only checked exceptions need documentation because the compiler handles those, and doclint passing proves the implementation matches the prose.
notes.production_context: A Java 21 API for ledger statements documents IOException for recoverable remote reads, NullPointerException for required keys and IndexOutOfBoundsException for invalid offsets, with tests and generated HTML.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 Javadoc supports @throws, @implSpec, links and doclint; generated HTML output still requires human semantic inspection and version-aware tool settings.
